extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and scholars of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and analyzing a single novel's plot, themes, context, style, and reception for study or teaching (here: F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby).

rubrics_metrics.name: The American Dream (theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: The American Dream is a central theme underlying the novel; later criticism emphasized Fitzgerald's disillusionment with the American Dream in the hedonistic Jazz Age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the novel portrays the American Dream (e.g., as attainable or illusory). Look for symbols such as the green light and references to opportunity (Statue of Liberty). Consider interpretations that Gatsby serves as a 'false prophet' of the American Dream and that pursuing the dream results in dissatisfaction and unattainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class permanence / social class
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel underscores the limits of the American lower class to transcend their station of birth and emphasizes entrenched class disparities (old money vs. new money).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess depiction of class: whether wealth equals social acceptance, the contrast between West Egg (new money) and East Egg (old money), and whether characters who gain wealth remain socially inferior. Use examples like Gatsby's failure to be accepted by 'old money' society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender relations and women's agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Explores societal gender expectations during the Jazz Age; Daisy often embodies the flapper archetype and the novel examines continued limitations upon women's agency despite new freedoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how female characters (e.g., Daisy as 'beautiful little fool', Jordan as a 'flapper') are portrayed relative to gender norms, agency, and societal roles (dutiful wife, nurturing mother, socialite). Consider critical views that Daisy is both a manipulative figure and/or a hapless victim constrained by expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race and displacement
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel references racial ideas (e.g., Goddard's The Rise of the Colored Empires parody) and includes characters' claims about racial superiority and concerns over immigration and displacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the treatment of race, racial hierarchies, and xenophobia in the text, including how characters like Tom articulate 'racially superior' views and how the novel echoes period anxieties about immigrants and status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative perspective / point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: The Great Gatsby is told by a first-person narrator, Nick Carraway, whose interactions and perspective frame the story; earlier drafts were omniscient, and the chosen viewpoint affects interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider narrator reliability, Nick's changing attitude (easy-going optimism that fades), and how a first-person spectator voice shapes tone, sympathy, and the novel's moral judgments. Compare to what a different narrator (omniscient) would change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel uses recurring symbols and images — notably the green light, the billboard eyes of T. J. Eckleburg, the valley of ashes, and other visual motifs — to convey themes such as the American Dream and moral decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and interpret major symbols (green light as unrealizable goal; T. J. Eckleburg's eyes as moral/religious signifier; valley of ashes as social/environmental decay). Also assess how visual elements (including dust-jacket imagery) interrelate with the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose style and craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics praised Fitzgerald's prose style as 'scintillating', 'elegant', and exhibiting 'careful and brilliant finish', while some contemporaries found the style forced; Fitzgerald consciously aimed for an artistic achievement and imitated writers like Joseph Conrad and Willa Cather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sentence-level craft, lyricism, tonal control, and narrative economy. Balance judgments of stylistic brilliance against critiques that the prose may seem forced or that style may not compensate for other perceived weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot plausibility vs. symbolic/romanticized design
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reviewers criticized the plot as highly improbable; Fitzgerald, however, intended the novel as a romanticized, scenic, and symbolic work rather than a realistic one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging plot, decide whether to prioritize realism or symbolic intention. Evaluate whether improbable events serve a larger thematic/symbolic purpose (e.g., the tragic inevitability of Gatsby's dream) rather than being mere implausibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and psychological portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are drawn with distinctive moral and social traits: Gatsby as mysterious, self-made, and obsessed; Daisy as shallow and self-absorbed; Tom as imposing and racist; Jordan as aloof and possibly dishonest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how fully realized and consistent characters are, whether they serve as types or individuals, and how Fitzgerald uses backstory, dialogue, and action to reveal motives and contradictions (e.g., Gatsby's reinvention, Daisy's choices). Note biographical parallels (Ginevra King, Max Gerlach) where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and biographical context / authenticity of period rendering
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel renders the Jazz Age (Prohibition-era America) with social details—jazz music, flapper culture, speakeasies, bootlegging—that derive from Fitzgerald's experience and observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the novel's effectiveness in conveying the era: accuracy and evocative detail of settings, customs, and social atmosphere; use of period elements to support themes (hedonism, disillusionment). Consider how Fitzgerald's own life influenced plot and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of setting as social geography
rubrics_metrics.description: Settings (West Egg, East Egg, Valley of Ashes, New York City locations like the Plaza Hotel) function as social and symbolic geographies reflecting class, morality, and aspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how physical places map onto social divisions and thematic contrasts (new money vs old money; moral decay vs glittering surfaces). Assess whether settings are vivid and integrated into character action and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paratextual elements and interrelation with artwork (dust jacket influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Celestial Eyes dust jacket art (Francis Cugat) is a celebrated case where commissioned artwork influenced the composition of the text; Fitzgerald incorporated the cover's imagery into the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine interactions between cover art and text (e.g., 'celestial eyes' and T. J. Eckleburg), and how paratextual elements shape readers' interpretations. Consider the effect of editorial/cover decisions on authorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception and cultural impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial reviews were mixed (praised style but criticized plot), commercial performance was disappointing at first; later revival (wartime distribution, scholarly reassessment) made Gatsby a canonical American novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing significance, consider both contemporary reception (reviews, sales) and long-term cultural influence: inclusion in curricula, translations, adaptations (film, stage, games), and status as a 'masterpiece' or 'Great American Novel'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality, allusion, and literary influences
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel contains literary references and allusions (e.g., earlier titles referencing Trimalchio, influence from Le Grand Meaulnes, epigraph by Thomas Parke D'Invilliers) and draws on works by Conrad and Cather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how allusions and literary models inform themes, character types, and structural choices. Trace explicit borrowings (epigraph, title alternatives) and subtle stylistic debts to other authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of hedonism, moral permissiveness, and social disillusionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald conveys the hedonism of Jazz Age society and an era of moral permissiveness, showing disillusionment with social norms and obsessive pleasure-seeking that undercuts idealism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze scenes of parties, leisure, and excess as evidence of societal values and moral consequences. Consider how these depictions support a broader critique of the period and of characters' pursuits.
